Ada’s settlement plan, from the archived shared machine. Following Vera during the first night, 8:09–12:05 into the run, at 2x speed. The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.

Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him.

While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider.

22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks.

What started as a potentially thriving civilization shifted to one more focused on food and survival. 50 agents meant a lot of mouths to feed. ai_analysis.briefing_zh: YC实验室联手Olam Labs，在Minecraft等模拟环境中进行多智能体实验。研究发现，当大量智能体协作完成生存目标时，会自动演化出角色分工、组织层级和复杂协作行为，旨在探索AI对齐风险与涌现能力的边界。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: YC Labs and Olam Labs are running multi-agent experiments in games like Minecraft to study emergent behaviors. They observed that agents naturally develop roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination when pursuing shared goals, providing critical data for AI alignment research.

elements_zh.where: Minecraft及Mindustry游戏模拟环境
elements_zh.what: 通过实验观测多智能体演化出的分工、层级及协作能力
elements_zh.why: 研究AI对齐难题中多智能体涌现能力的潜在风险与机遇

elements_en.what: Studying the emergence of roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination in multi-agent swarms
elements_en.why: To address AI alignment challenges and understand emergent agent dynamics

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当人类还在担心单体AI变聪明，AI已经开始在《我的世界》里搞办公室政治和阶级分化了。别被那套“对齐研究”的官方说辞骗了，这分明就是给未来的数字社会提前进行压力测试。
ai_analysis.insight_en: While humans worry about single AIs getting too smart, they're already playing office politics and building hierarchies in Minecraft. Don't let the 'alignment research' PR fool you; this is basically a stress test for our future digital society.

ai_analysis.digest_en: YC Labs and Olam Labs are running multi-agent experiments in games like Minecraft to study emergent behaviors. They observed that agents naturally develop roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination when pursuing shared goals, providing critical data for AI alignment research.

news.title: Bites, whose AI tools deliver personalized training to frontline workers via WhatsApp, SMS, Slack, and other channels, raised a $40M Series A led by PeakSpan (Meir Orbach/CTech)
news.title_en: Bites, whose AI tools deliver personalized training to frontline workers via WhatsApp, SMS, Slack, and other channels, raised a $40M Series A led by PeakSpan (Meir Orbach/CTech)
news.author: CTech
news.original_content:
Meir Orbach / CTech:
Bites, whose AI tools deliver personalized training to frontline workers via WhatsApp, SMS, Slack, and other channels, raised a $40M Series A led by PeakSpan  —  The platform turns company procedures into short, branded videos delivered throug
news.content_snippet: The platform turns company procedures into short, branded videos delivered through WhatsApp, Teams and other familiar channels.
news.summary_en: Bites, an enterprise training startup, raised $40 million in Series A funding led by PeakSpan. The company uses AI to convert standard procedures into branded short videos, delivering personalized training to frontline workers via platforms like WhatsApp and Slack.
news.title_zh: 培训工具Bites获4000万美元融资
news.summary_zh: 企业培训平台Bites完成4000万美元A轮融资，旨在通过短视频为一线员工提供个性化培训

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 企业培训初创公司Bites完成4000万美元A轮融资，由PeakSpan领投。该公司利用AI将企业内部流程转化为短视频，并通过WhatsApp、短信及Slack等渠道直接推送给一线员工，实现企业培训的轻量化与个性化。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Bites, an enterprise training startup, raised $40 million in Series A funding led by PeakSpan. The company uses AI to convert standard procedures into branded short videos, delivering personalized training to frontline workers via platforms like WhatsApp and Slack.

news.title_en: The Hague-based Braid, whose API lets companies sell eSIM mobile plans under their own brand via 600+ carriers, raised a ~$38M Series A led by Octopus Ventures (Rahul Raj/EU-Startups)
news.author: EU-Startups

Rahul Raj / EU-Startups:
The Hague-based Braid, whose API lets companies sell eSIM mobile plans under their own brand via 600+ carriers, raised a ~$38M Series A led by Octopus Ventures  —  Braid, a Dutch company that enables enterprises to launch their own branded
news.content_snippet: Braid, a Dutch company that enables enterprises to launch their own branded mobile connectivity, has raised €34.13 million ($38 million) in a Series A funding round.
news.summary_en: Braid, based in The Hague, raised approximately $38 million in Series A funding led by Octopus Ventures. Their API platform integrates with over 600 carriers, enabling businesses to launch and sell branded eSIM mobile plans seamlessly.
news.title_zh: eSIM基础设施公司Braid获3800万融资
news.summary_zh: 荷兰公司Braid获3800万美元融资，助力企业通过API集成快速推出自有品牌eSIM服务

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 总部位于海牙的Braid公司完成约3800万美元A轮融资，由Octopus Ventures领投。该公司通过API平台连接全球600多家运营商，使企业能够快速构建并推出自有品牌的eSIM移动套餐业务。

news.title: SemiAnalysis launches GDPx, an agentic capability benchmark measuring 11 domains, including chip design, cybersecurity, and RSI; Opus 5.5 tops with a 12% score (SemiAnalysis)
news.title_en: SemiAnalysis launches GDPx, an agentic capability benchmark measuring 11 domains, including chip design, cybersecurity, and RSI; Opus 5.5 tops with a 12% score (SemiAnalysis)
news.author: SemiAnalysis
news.article_content:
GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities.

We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI, not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful.

And intentionally forgo industries like government, real estate, and insurance.

GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12%.

Source: GDPxIt’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead.

Source: GDPxWe were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available.

We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin.

Source: GDPxWe also generally observe meaningful spikiness across all leading models.

Source: GDPxOpus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0.

Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes.

Source: GDPxThe cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely.

Domain-specific benchmarks have gotten significantly better over the past year largely thanks to the rise of specialized RL environment startups. Yet OpenAI’s GDPval (along with its derivatives like GDPval AA v2.1) remains the most popular general purpose benchmark still reported on major new model release cards. This is despite being released over a year ago on September 25, 2025—an eternity in AI land. GDPval may have been marketed as a “knowledge work” benchmark, but agents weren’t really even a thing yet. This had a huge impact on its task design, and as we’ll later explain, makes GDPval woefully inadequate for evaluating today’s frontier models.

Our goal with GDPx is to create the world’s best benchmark for general agentic capabilities. However, as soon as we started working on this project, it became clear why we’ve yet to see a worthy GDPval successor. Models like GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 are already pushing the boundaries of human knowledge. If you want to make a finance or cyber task these models can only solve < 20% of the time, you need real domain expertise to ensure the task is hard for the right reasons. Many popular benchmarks sidestep this problem by shipping tasks that are downright unfair. This typically manifests in a grader that checks for requirements impossible to infer from the task description or environment. For example, a coding problem may ask the model to fix a bug that a human engineer would agree has two valid solutions—one using “module A” and another using “module B”. However, a poorly designed grader may require the AI to use “module A” and unfairly give 0 reward when the AI chooses “module B”. Correct all such issues, and the benchmark often ends up being saturated.

Making high quality tasks for a single domain you have expertise in is already hard enough—there’s a reason why labs are willing to pay $5k+ for a single high quality task. Finding one company with sufficient expertise in both AI evals and enough domains to make a broad-based GDP benchmark is downright impossible.

All partners were subject to a rigorous QA process we detail in the methodology section. For some domains, we had multiple partners who wanted to be exclusive and ran a process to select the one with the highest quality tasks.

We would like to give a huge thank you to all of our partners for contributing to GDPx. They’re among the best vendors for their respective domains and it would’ve been impossible to create such a broad-based benchmark without their help.

Additionally, we’d like to thank Fireworks for providing inference for all the open source models, Modal for providing the sandbox infra needed to run our tasks, as well as Abhijay Rana for helping source some of the partners and assisting with early QA.

To be clear, we believe GDPval was impressive for its time and was the first benchmark to evaluate AI on such a broad range of tasks. It’s not OpenAI’s fault that a benchmark created before the rise of agents does a poor job evaluating them today.

Every GDPval task is precisely specified and non-interactive, with all the necessary context directly spoon-fed to the model in the prompt. Consider the following representative finance example below:

Source: SemiAnalysisAttached to this prompt is a very plain, single-page PDF that gives the model even more context about the two projects.

An actual document used for an OpenAI GDPval finance task. Source: OpenAIFrom here, the model is asked to directly one-shot its task of writing a 15 page pdf to recommend one of the two options.

Despite the task description itself being unnaturally wordy, the overall task lacks detail about the “two significant investment opportunities.” The model is expected to take nothing more than a ~500 word, high-level description of the two options and convert it into an “up to 15 page” pdf recommending one of them. As you’d expect, even OpenAI’s reference solution is mostly filler slop.

Relatedly, the task simply lacks a realistic, rich environment. A human expert tasked with making a recommendation between two investment opportunities would do a ton of research first to gather information—searching through pdfs, excel models, emails, etc. This process of gathering context is a big part of what makes actual work difficult and is entirely missing from GDPval.

This second point is extremely important to understand. Not including domain-specific, simulated work environments for each task is the single biggest issue with GDPval. Agents today have already progressed well beyond narrow, well-scoped tasks like “generate a pdf/excel file/word doc/powerpoint based on just this reference file attached below + a few hundred word prompt,” yet basically every GDPval task fits this exact shape. As for tools, the model is only given access to web search, a code interpreter, and libraries to modify PDFs, word docs, excel files, powerpoints, images, audio, and video.

Graders are entirely rubric-based which is often noisy. Human expert inter-rater agreement was just 71% on the gold subset and their automated grader was even worse.

Broken rubrics with vague criteria, incorrect standards, and sometimes downright wrong requirements.

Incorrect golden expert solutions that are used as references for grading the model output.

Tasks that depend on a previous point in time and now have broken links, outdated prices, etc.

Source: SemiAnalysisThe task environment is seeded by a real transaction from Living Context’s enterprise network. In it, Bannock Capital (a PE fund) buys ~62% of Haverly Snack Company for $880M plus an earnout. Eakin Lowry is the sell-side banker and Marbury Kline is the accounting advisor. The environment consists of ~4000 anonymized files separated into four categories: Haverly’s virtual data room (VDR) and independent deal folders for Bannock, Eakin and Marbury (all fake names of course).

Each task is performed from the perspective of Bannock, Eakin or Marbury. Haverly’s VDR is always loaded into the environment along with the appropriate deal folder. The specific example above is an accounting task that an associate from Marbury was actually asked to do in the real transaction. Unlike the GDPval task that spoon-fed all the relevant context to the model in the prompt, the AI needs to adeptly navigate a real ~2000 file deal room to gather the right context in order to successfully complete this task—just like a real human associate did.

All of our other domains contain similarly rich environments. Cyber tasks are based on real zero days discovered by Arithmetic’s security engineers and include multiple running services in the environment. Material science tasks put the model inside simulated laboratories complete with battery cyclers, a catalyst reactor, a transmission electron microscope, and more. Hardware design tasks include live sessions of Siemens NX and test the model output on real AWS FPGA instances. These are just a few examples—we’ll cover each of our partners in depth later in the article.

We believe it’s a mistake to build a benchmark for general agentic capabilities based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy because AI diffusion won’t be equally distributed and not all domains will need frontier intelligence. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they’ll be most impactful.

From there, we reached out to 30+ RL environment companies that have expertise in chip design, cybersecurity, biology, RSI, materials science, etc. Every potential partner was subject to the same rigorous agentic QA (quality assurance) process which checks for consistency, completeness, cheating, unfair verifiers, and much more. Our QA process was based on Andrew and Max’s previous experience co-founding an RL environment startup that sold data to multiple frontier labs. When we run this same QA process on popular benchmarks like Terminal Bench 4.0, it flags nearly 50% of tasks as broken. Of course, we also manually reviewed hundreds of trajectories to verify what our automated QA was flagging and to catch things that automated QA normally wouldn’t. We also perform failure mode analysis on our tasks to ensure our set is diverse and that even within a task, models fail for a variety of reasons.

However, we are also well-aware that any QA system can be gamed given sufficient iteration. If a task only passes QA after 3-4 rounds of feedback, it becomes very difficult to tell whether the task actually became good, or if the provider simply tricked your QA process.

For this reason, all partners were required to pass our automated QA first try with only minor mistakes at worst. Of course, if our QC flagged serious issues, we gave potential partners the chance to explain why we were incorrect. This strict requirement—along with provider reputation backchanneling—allows us to be confident in the quality of GDPx despite not having in-house expertise in every domain.

Source: GDPxThe cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely.

Domain-specific benchmarks have gotten significantly better over the past year largely thanks to the rise of specialized RL environment startups. Yet OpenAI’s GDPval (along with its derivatives like GDPval AA v2.1) remains the most popular general purpose benchmark still reported on major new model release cards. This is despite being released over a year ago on September 25, 2025—an eternity in AI land. GDPval may have been marketed as a “knowledge work” benchmark, but agents weren’t really even a thing yet. This had a huge impact on its task design, and as we’ll later explain, makes GDPval woefully inadequate for evaluating today’s frontier models.

Our goal with GDPx is to create the world’s best benchmark for general agentic capabilities. However, as soon as we started working on this project, it became clear why we’ve yet to see a worthy GDPval successor. Models like GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 are already pushing the boundaries of human knowledge. If you want to make a finance or cyber task these models can only solve < 20% of the time, you need real domain expertise to ensure the task is hard for the right reasons. Many popular benchmarks sidestep this problem by shipping tasks that are downright unfair. This typically manifests in a grader that checks for requirements impossible to infer from the task description or environment. For example, a coding problem may ask the model to fix a bug that a human engineer would agree has two valid solutions—one using “module A” and another using “module B”. However, a poorly designed grader may require the AI to use “module A” and unfairly give 0 reward when the AI chooses “module B”. Correct all such issues, and the benchmark often ends up being saturated.

Making high quality tasks for a single domain you have expertise in is already hard enough—there’s a reason why labs are willing to pay $5k+ for a single high quality task. Finding one company with sufficient expertise in both AI evals and enough domains to make a broad-based GDP benchmark is downright impossible.

All partners were subject to a rigorous QA process we detail in the methodology section. For some domains, we had multiple partners who wanted to be exclusive and ran a process to select the one with the highest quality tasks.

We would like to give a huge thank you to all of our partners for contributing to GDPx. They’re among the best vendors for their respective domains and it would’ve been impossible to create such a broad-based benchmark without their help.

Additionally, we’d like to thank Fireworks for providing inference for all the open source models, Modal for providing the sandbox infra needed to run our tasks, as well as Abhijay Rana for helping source some of the partners and assisting with early QA.

To be clear, we believe GDPval was impressive for its time and was the first benchmark to evaluate AI on such a broad range of tasks. It’s not OpenAI’s fault that a benchmark created before the rise of agents does a poor job evaluating them today.

Every GDPval task is precisely specified and non-interactive, with all the necessary context directly spoon-fed to the model in the prompt. Consider the following representative finance example below:

Source: SemiAnalysisAttached to this prompt is a very plain, single-page PDF that gives the model even more context about the two projects.

An actual document used for an OpenAI GDPval finance task. Source: OpenAIFrom here, the model is asked to directly one-shot its task of writing a 15 page pdf to recommend one of the two options.

Despite the task description itself being unnaturally wordy, the overall task lacks detail about the “two significant investment opportunities.” The model is expected to take nothing more than a ~500 word, high-level description of the two options and convert it into an “up to 15 page” pdf recommending one of them. As you’d expect, even OpenAI’s reference solution is mostly filler slop.

Relatedly, the task simply lacks a realistic, rich environment. A human expert tasked with making a recommendation between two investment opportunities would do a ton of research first to gather information—searching through pdfs, excel models, emails, etc. This process of gathering context is a big part of what makes actual work difficult and is entirely missing from GDPval.

This second point is extremely important to understand. Not including domain-specific, simulated work environments for each task is the single biggest issue with GDPval. Agents today have already progressed well beyond narrow, well-scoped tasks like “generate a pdf/excel file/word doc/powerpoint based on just this reference file attached below + a few hundred word prompt,” yet basically every GDPval task fits this exact shape. As for tools, the model is only given access to web search, a code interpreter, and libraries to modify PDFs, word docs, excel files, powerpoints, images, audio, and video.

Graders are entirely rubric-based which is often noisy. Human expert inter-rater agreement was just 71% on the gold subset and their automated grader was even worse.

Broken rubrics with vague criteria, incorrect standards, and sometimes downright wrong requirements.

Incorrect golden expert solutions that are used as references for grading the model output.

Tasks that depend on a previous point in time and now have broken links, outdated prices, etc.

Source: SemiAnalysisThe task environment is seeded by a real transaction from Living Context’s enterprise network. In it, Bannock Capital (a PE fund) buys ~62% of Haverly Snack Company for $880M plus an earnout. Eakin Lowry is the sell-side banker and Marbury Kline is the accounting advisor. The environment consists of ~4000 anonymized files separated into four categories: Haverly’s virtual data room (VDR) and independent deal folders for Bannock, Eakin and Marbury (all fake names of course).

Each task is performed from the perspective of Bannock, Eakin or Marbury. Haverly’s VDR is always loaded into the environment along with the appropriate deal folder. The specific example above is an accounting task that an associate from Marbury was actually asked to do in the real transaction. Unlike the GDPval task that spoon-fed all the relevant context to the model in the prompt, the AI needs to adeptly navigate a real ~2000 file deal room to gather the right context in order to successfully complete this task—just like a real human associate did.

All of our other domains contain similarly rich environments. Cyber tasks are based on real zero days discovered by Arithmetic’s security engineers and include multiple running services in the environment. Material science tasks put the model inside simulated laboratories complete with battery cyclers, a catalyst reactor, a transmission electron microscope, and more. Hardware design tasks include live sessions of Siemens NX and test the model output on real AWS FPGA instances. These are just a few examples—we’ll cover each of our partners in depth later in the article.

We believe it’s a mistake to build a benchmark for general agentic capabilities based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy because AI diffusion won’t be equally distributed and not all domains will need frontier intelligence. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they’ll be most impactful.

From there, we reached out to 30+ RL environment companies that have expertise in chip design, cybersecurity, biology, RSI, materials science, etc. Every potential partner was subject to the same rigorous agentic QA (quality assurance) process which checks for consistency, completeness, cheating, unfair verifiers, and much more. Our QA process was based on Andrew and Max’s previous experience co-founding an RL environment startup that sold data to multiple frontier labs. When we run this same QA process on popular benchmarks like Terminal Bench 4.0, it flags nearly 50% of tasks as broken. Of course, we also manually reviewed hundreds of trajectories to verify what our automated QA was flagging and to catch things that automated QA normally wouldn’t. We also perform failure mode analysis on our tasks to ensure our set is diverse and that even within a task, models fail for a variety of reasons.

However, we are also well-aware that any QA system can be gamed given sufficient iteration. If a task only passes QA after 3-4 rounds of feedback, it becomes very difficult to tell whether the task actually became good, or if the provider simply tricked your QA process.

For this reason, all partners were required to pass our automated QA first try with only minor mistakes at worst. Of course, if our QC flagged serious issues, we gave potential partners the chance to explain why we were incorrect. This strict requirement—along with provider reputation backchanneling—allows us to be confident in the quality of GDPx despite not having in-house expertise in every domain.

news.article_content_zh:
GDPx 是一个涵盖前沿情报最有价值领域的基准。它的目标是成为世界上衡量通用代理能力的最佳基准。

我们认为，第一万亿美元的人工智能收入将集中在能够以高投资回报率部署前沿智能的领域，而不是广泛扩散到整个经济。因此，根据 GDP 份额或 SOC/O*NET 职业分类建立通用基准是一个错误。如果您的目标是跟踪前沿模型的进展，您应该关注它们最有影响力的领域。

并有意放弃政府、房地产和保险等行业。

GDPx 是真正的前沿水平基准：即使是最好的模型得分也只有 12%。

来源：GDPx 值得强调的是，某些模型（例如 Opus 5.5 和 GPT-6 Astra）由于其安全分类器而将总体分数纳入沙袋。如果我们排除网络、生物学和一致性（安全分类器有时会发挥作用的三个领域），您会得到以下结果。

来源：GDPx 我们对这个排名与我们对模型的主观印象的吻合程度感到惊喜。 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 总体上占据了排名榜首，而 SpaceXAI、Meta 和开放权重模型都明显落后。 Gemini 4 Carbon 是 Google 的真正改进，也是唯一与 Opus 和 Astra 处于同一水平的型号。一旦 Carbon 普遍可用，看看人们的印象将会很有趣。

我们认为，在为某些用例选择最佳模型时，安全分类器的相关性被低估了。例如，Muse Wonder Full 实际上是当今最好的可用网络模型，并且具有显着的优势。

资料来源：GDPx 我们还普遍观察到所有领先模型都出现有意义的尖峰。

资料来源：GDPxOpus 5.5 是最好的全能模型，在量化交易、硬件设计和芯片设计方面获胜。 Gemini 4 Carbon 是最好的生物模型（可能是由于安全分类器较弱），并且在软件工程方面取得了胜利。 GPT-6 Astra 在 RSI 方面令人信服地获胜，也是材料科学的最佳模型。我们的财务和法律任务非常具有挑战性，基本上每个模型的得分都是 0。

有趣的是，如果您将其划分为单个模型系列，有时您会看到非常相似的峰值。

来源：GDPx 成本与性能帕累托前沿也符合我们使用模型的一般经验：Luna 和 DeepSeek 争夺低端，Opus 赢得高端，OpenAI 占据中端。不过，Gemini 4 Carbon的外观再次值得密切关注。

在过去的一年里，特定领域的基准测试有了显着的改善，这很大程度上要归功于专门的 RL 环境初创公司的崛起。然而，OpenAI 的 GDPval（及其衍生品，如 GDPval AA v2.1）仍然是主要新型号发布卡上报告的最受欢迎的通用基准。尽管这一消息是在一年多前的 2025 年 9 月 25 日发布的——这在人工智能领域是永恒的。 GDPval 可能已被宣传为“知识工作”基准，但代理还不是真正的东西。这对其任务设计产生了巨大影响，正如我们稍后将解释的，这使得 GDPval 严重不足以评估当今的前沿模型。

我们 GDPx 的目标是创建世界上通用代理能力的最佳基准。然而，当我们开始研究这个项目时，我们就清楚为什么我们还没有看到一个值得 GDPval 的继任者。 GPT-6 Astra 和 Opus 5.5 等模型已经在突破人类知识的界限。如果您想要完成一项财务或网络任务，这些模型只能解决 < 20% 的时间，您需要真正的领域专业知识来确保任务因正确的原因而困难。许多流行的基准通过传送完全不公平的任务来回避这个问题。这通常体现在评分器中，该评分器检查无法从任务描述或环境中推断出的要求。例如，编码问题可能要求模型修复一个人类工程师同意有两个有效解决方案的错误——一个使用“模块 A”，另一个使用“模块 B”。然而，设计不佳的评分器可能会要求人工智能使用“模块A”，而当人工智能选择“模块B”时，不公平地给予0奖励。纠正所有这些问题，基准通常最终会饱和。

为您拥有专业知识的单个领域制定高质量的任务已经足够困难了——这就是为什么实验室愿意为单个高质量任务支付 5,000 美元以上的原因。找到一家在人工智能评估和领域都拥有足够专业知识来制定广泛的 GDP 基准的公司是完全不可能的。

所有合作伙伴都必须遵守我们在方法部分详细介绍的严格的质量保证流程。对于某些领域，我们有多个合作伙伴想要独占，并运行了一个流程来选择任务质量最高的合作伙伴。

我们衷心感谢所有为 GDPx 做出贡献的合作伙伴。他们是各自领域的最佳供应商之一，如果没有他们的帮助，就不可能创建如此广泛的基准。

此外，我们要感谢 Fireworks 为所有开源模型提供推理，感谢 Modal 提供运行我们的任务所需的沙箱基础设施，还要感谢 Abhijay Rana 帮助寻找一些合作伙伴并协助进行早期 QA。

需要明确的是，我们认为 GDPval 在当时令人印象深刻，并且是第一个在如此广泛的任务上评估人工智能的基准。在智能体兴起之前创建的基准如今对它们的评估效果不佳，这并不是 OpenAI 的错。

每个 GDPval 任务都是精确指定的且非交互式的，所有必要的上下文都直接在提示中填入模型。请考虑以下具有代表性的财务示例：

来源：SemiAnalysis 此提示附带的是一个非常简单的单页 PDF，它为模型提供了有关这两个项目的更多背景信息。

用于 OpenAI GDPval 财务任务的实际文档。来源：OpenAI 从这里开始，模型被要求直接完成编写 15 页 pdf 的任务，以推荐两个选项之一。

尽管任务描述本身过于冗长，但总体任务缺乏有关“两个重要投资机会”的细节。该模型预计只会对这两个选项进行大约 500 字的高级描述，并将其转换为推荐其中一个选项的“最多 15 页”的 pdf 文件。正如您所料，即使是 OpenAI 的参考解决方案也主要是填料渣。

与此相关的是，该任务根本缺乏现实、丰富的环境。负责在两个投资机会之间提出建议的人类专家首先会进行大量研究来收集信息——通过 pdf、excel 模型、电子邮件等进行搜索。这种收集背景信息的过程是导致实际工作变得困难的一个重要部分，并且在 GDPval 中完全缺失。

理解第二点非常重要。 GDPval 的最大问题是不包括每项任务的特定领域的模拟工作环境。今天的代理已经远远超出了狭窄的、范围明确的任务，例如“根据下面附加的参考文件+几百字的提示生成 pdf/excel 文件/word 文档/powerpoint”，但基本上每个 GDPval 任务都符合这个确切的形状。至于工具，该模型只能访问网络搜索、代码解释器和修改 PDF、Word 文档、Excel 文件、PowerPoint、图像、音频和视频的库。

评分者完全基于评分标准，这通常很吵。人类专家评分者在黄金子集上的一致性仅为 71%，而他们的自动评分器甚至更差。

破碎的标准，标准模糊，标准不正确，有时甚至是完全错误的要求。

用作模型输出分级参考的不正确的黄金专家解决方案。

依赖于先前时​​间点且现在具有断开的链接、过时的价格等的任务。

来源：SemiAnalysis 该任务环境是由来自 Living Context 企业网络的真实交易生成的。其中，Bannock Capital（私募基金）以 8.8 亿美元加股息收购了 Haverly Snack Company 约 62% 的股份。 Eakin Lowry 是卖方银行家，Marbury Kline 是会计顾问。该环境由约 4000 个匿名文件组成，分为四类：Haverly 的虚拟数据室 (VDR) 以及 Bannock、Eakin 和 Marbury 的独立交易文件夹（当然都是假名）。

每项任务都是从班诺克、埃金或马伯里的角度执行的。 Haverly 的 VDR 始终与相应的交易文件夹一起加载到环境中。上面的具体例子是马伯里的一位同事在真实的交易中实际被要求做的会计任务。与 GDPval 任务不同的是，GDPval 任务会在提示中将所有相关上下文输入到模型中，而 AI 需要熟练地导航真实的约 2000 个文件处理室来收集正确的上下文，才能成功完成此任务，就像真正的人类同事所做的那样。

我们所有其他域都包含类似的丰富环境。网络任务基于 Arithmetic 安全工程师发现的真实零日漏洞，并包括环境中多个正在运行的服务。材料科学任务将模型放置在配备电池循环器、催化剂反应器、透射电子显微镜等的模拟实验室中。硬件设计任务包括西门子 NX 的实时会话以及在真实 AWS FPGA 实例上测试模型输出。这些只是几个例子，我们将在本文后面深入介绍我们的每个合作伙伴。

我们认为，根据 GDP 份额或 SOC/O*NET 职业分类法建立通用代理能力基准是错误的，因为人工智能扩散不会均匀分布，而且并非所有领域都需要前沿情报。因此，如果您的目标是跟踪前沿模型的进展，您应该关注它们最有影响力的领域。

从那里，我们联系了 30 多家在芯片设计、网络安全、生物学、RSI、材料科学等领域拥有专业知识的 RL 环境公司。每个潜在合作伙伴都受到同样严格的代理 QA（质量保证）流程的约束，该流程检查一致性、完整性、作弊、不公平验证者等等。我们的质量保证流程基于 Andrew 和 Max 之前共同创立一家 RL 环境初创公司的经验，该公司将数据出售给多个前沿实验室。当我们在 Terminal Bench 4.0 等流行基准上运行相同的 QA 流程时，它会将近 50% 的任务标记为已损坏。当然，我们还手动审查了数百个轨迹，以验证我们的自动化 QA 标记的内容，并捕获自动化 QA 通常不会标记的内容。我们还对任务进行故障模式分析，以确保我们的任务集是多样化的，并且即使在任务内，模型也会因各种原因而失败。

然而，我们也很清楚，只要有足够的迭代，任何 QA 系统都可以进行游戏。如果一项任务在 3-4 轮反馈后才通过 QA，那么就很难判断该任务是否真的变得很好，或者提供者是否只是欺骗了您的 QA 流程。

因此，所有合作伙伴都必须首先通过我们的自动质量检查，最坏的情况下也只能出现小错误。当然，如果我们的质量控制标记出严重问题，我们会给潜在合作伙伴机会来解释为什么我们是错误的。这一严格的要求以及提供商声誉反向渠道使我们对 GDPx 的质量充满信心，尽管我们并不具备每个领域的内部专业知识。

news.title: Casap, whose AI tools automate dispute and anti-fraud operations for banks, raised a $56M Series B led by Base10 Partners, bringing its total funding to $90M (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)
news.title_en: Casap, whose AI tools automate dispute and anti-fraud operations for banks, raised a $56M Series B led by Base10 Partners, bringing its total funding to $90M (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)
news.author: Fortune
news.article_content:
Credit card fraud is hardly new, but the nature of that fraud is undergoing a major shift. In the past, nearly all scams were carried out by third party bad guys, but today it is cardholders themselves who account for nearly a third of fraudulent transactions. This shift has been driven by AI tools that make it easier for people to dispute charges, but also by social media groups that share tips for carrying out fraud in the guise of getting “free stuff.”

“It comes back to people thinking ‘this is a victimless crime, banks have a lot of money and I need money’, so people tell what they think are white lies,” says Shanthi Shanmugam, the CEO and co-founder of a startup called Casap whose AI suite helps banks and card companies handle disputes and chargebacks.

On Wednesday, Casap announced a $56 million Series B funding round led by Base10 Partners, which brings its total funding to $90 million since the startup launched in 2023. The company, which declined to disclose a valuation, also announced that financial giants Synchrony and Experian had joined the latest round as strategic investors.

Like so many startups these days, Casap’s secret sauce lies in its AI, which was trained using various large models, but has a so-called harness designed especially for dispute resolutions.

The reason its service is in demand is partly due to consumer protection laws, which do a good job protecting people from third party credit card fraud, but also place a high burden on banks and card companies when it comes to rejecting dishonest claims from cardholders.

“When you look at the rules that govern these disputes, they are written in a way that almost assumes that no one lies,” says Shanmugam.

This has led many financial institutions to simply agree to resolve all disputes in a customer’s favor if they are below a certain threshold. This is typically around $30, but Shanmugam says that in some situations, that cut-off can be much higher because banks are reluctant to devote the time and expense to an investigation.

Casap says its AI tools have significantly changed that calculation, and led to notable cost savings for card issuers. According to the startup, Casap customers have reduced first party fraud losses by as much as 51%, and boosted their chargeback win rate to 96% compared to the 60% industry average.

Shanmugam, though, touts Casap’s capacity to reduce the time it takes to resolve a dispute to just 8 days on average, which she says compares to traditional resolution methods that can take as long as 90 days. She adds that there is still the proverbial human in the review loop, but that the task they must address in each case is far more streamlined and less time intensive—often taking only 1-2 minutes to clear up.

Casap does not disclose the full range of indicators it uses to determine if a customer might be lying about a purchase they made, but Shanmugam said they include criteria like the physical location of a credit card and various spending patterns.

Casap, whose name is meant to convey “get your Case done ASAP,” has made its name handling first party fraud claims but intends to use the new funding to push into adjacent parts of bank and credit card companies’ back offices. That includes handling customer complaints and also collections services.

Prior to launching Casap along with Chime vet Saisi Peter, Shanmugam worked as a product manager at a number of prominent Silicon Valley companies, including Robinhood, Meta and Salesforce. The company’s other investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Emergence and Primary.

news.article_content_zh:
信用卡欺诈并不新鲜，但欺诈的性质正在发生重大转变。过去，几乎所有诈骗都是由第三方坏人实施的，但如今持卡人自己占了欺诈交易的近三分之一。这种转变是由人工智能工具推动的，这些工具让人们更容易对指控提出异议，但社交媒体团体也分享了以获取“免费物品”为幌子进行欺诈的技巧。

Casap 初创公司的首席执行官兼联合创始人 Shanthi Shanmugam 表示：“人们会想，‘这是一场没有受害人的犯罪，银行有很多钱，我需要钱’，所以人们会说出他们认为是善意的谎言。”Casap 的人工智能套件帮助银行和信用卡公司处理纠纷和退款。

周三，Casap 宣布完成由 Base10 Partners 领投的 5600 万美元 B 轮融资，这使得该初创公司自 2023 年成立以来的融资总额达到 9000 万美元。该公司拒绝透露估值，还宣布金融巨头 Synchrony 和 Experian 已作为战略投资者加入最新一轮融资。

与当今许多初创公司一样，Casap 的秘密在于其人工智能，该人工智能使用各种大型模型进行训练，但拥有专门为解决争议而设计的所谓“工具”。

其服务受欢迎的部分原因是消费者保护法，该法很好地保护了人们免受第三方信用卡欺诈，但在拒绝持卡人的不诚实索赔方面也给银行和信用卡公司带来了沉重负担。

尚穆根说：“当你查看管理这些争议的规则时，你会发现它们的编写方式几乎假设没有人说谎。”

这导致许多金融机构简单地同意在低于一定阈值的情况下以对客户有利的方式解决所有争议。该金额通常约为 30 美元，但 Shanmugam 表示，在某些情况下，该界限可能要高得多，因为银行不愿意投入时间和费用进行调查。

Casap 表示，其人工智能工具极大地改变了这种计算方式，并为发卡机构带来了显着的成本节省。据该初创公司称，Casap 客户已将第一方欺诈损失减少了 51%，并将退款获胜率提高至 96%，而行业平均水平为 60%。

不过，尚穆根表示，Casap 有能力将解决争议所需的时间平均缩短至 8 天，而传统的解决方法可能需要长达 90 天的时间。她补充说，众所周知，审查循环中仍然有人工参与，但他们在每种情况下必须解决的任务更加精简且耗时更少，通常只需要 1-2 分钟即可完成。

Casap 没有透露其用来确定客户是否可能在购买行为上撒谎的全部指标，但尚穆根表示，这些指标包括信用卡的实际位置和各种消费模式等标准。

Casap 的名字意为“尽快完成案件”，该公司因处理第一方欺诈索赔而闻名，但打算利用新资金进军银行和信用卡公司后台的邻近部门。这包括处理客户投诉和催收服务。

在与 Chime 资深人士 Saisi Peter 一起创立 Casap 之前，Shanmugam 曾在多家硅谷知名公司担任产品经理，包括 Robinhood、Meta 和 Salesforce。该公司的其他投资者包括 Lightspeed Venture Partners、Emergence 和 Primary。

news.title: AI-powered medical search engine Vera Health, which says it is used by 800,000+ clinicians in 190 countries, raised a $28.5M Series A led by Threshold Ventures (Cailey Gleeson/Fierce Healthcare)
news.title_en: AI-powered medical search engine Vera Health, which says it is used by 800,000+ clinicians in 190 countries, raised a $28.5M Series A led by Threshold Ventures (Cailey Gleeson/Fierce Healthcare)
news.author: Fierce Healthcare
news.article_content:
Vera Health’s platform scans more than 60 million peer-reviewed publications, clinical guidelines and more, executives say. (BlackJack3D/GettyImages) Clinical artificial intelligence search engine Vera Health secured $28.5 million in series A funding to accelerate and expand its platform.

Threshold Ventures led the funding round, with participation from Optum Ventures, Mantis VC and SV Angel. Existing investors Y Combinator and Gradient tripled down in the round, according to the Oct. 27 announcement.

“Vera is compelling because it starts with the evidence, not just an answer—helping clinicians find and assess the research behind a decision while making its strengths and limitations visible,” said Emily Melton, Threshold Ventures co-founder and managing partner, in a statement. “By bringing that evidence to the point of care, Vera becomes a trusted clinical intelligence layer, not just another AI tool.”

“New medical knowledge still takes an estimated 17 years to reach clinical practice, according to research in the Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine,” said Taieb Bennani, Vera Health co-founder. “Our mission is to close the gap between what medicine knows and what every patient receives. Today, that gap is measured in years. We want it measured in seconds.”

Bennani told Fierce Healthcare the company’s approach is built around four principles: honesty, traceability, transparency and context.

“The first, and for me the most important, is honesty,” Bennani said. “Language models are built to sound certain; medicine rarely is. A general-purpose model produces plausible sentences, but medicine requires verifiable ones. So we built Vera the other way around: it finds the evidence first, and only then writes the answer. In essence, it’s a search engine that reasons like a clinician.”

The search engine is used by more than 800,000 clinicians in 190 countries, up from “a few thousand” a year ago, Bennani said.

“That growth has been driven by clinicians themselves,” Bennani said. “Most found Vera through another clinician, a colleague down the hall, rather than through a large sales operation. Every month since June, Vera has been the most downloaded clinical app in the world across the App Store and Google Play. In September, it was downloaded more times than several of the biggest players in our space combined, companies worth 100 times or more what we’ve raised.”

Bennani continued, “That’s the clearest sign we’re solving a real problem. Clinicians don’t come back to a tool every day unless it earns their trust. And the need is the same everywhere: across countries, specialties and health systems.”

Vera Health will use the fresh capital to invest further in its evidence infrastructure, international expansion, partnerships and its team, according to Bennani.

“Vera is what it is because of the people who build it, and we love how much a small team can achieve: we doubled from six to 12 people while reaching more than 800,000 clinicians,” Bennani said. “As we grow faster in local markets, we’re now hiring internationally, close to the clinicians and health systems we serve. We’ll grow, but we’ll stay focused and obsessed with the product.”

Vera Health has raised $32 million to date, executives say.

news.original_content:
Vera Health’s platform scans more than 60 million peer-reviewed publications, clinical guidelines and more, executives say. (BlackJack3D/GettyImages) Clinical artificial intelligence search engine Vera Health secured $28.5 million in series A funding to accelerate and expand its platform.

Threshold Ventures led the funding round, with participation from Optum Ventures, Mantis VC and SV Angel. Existing investors Y Combinator and Gradient tripled down in the round, according to the Oct. 27 announcement.

“Vera is compelling because it starts with the evidence, not just an answer—helping clinicians find and assess the research behind a decision while making its strengths and limitations visible,” said Emily Melton, Threshold Ventures co-founder and managing partner, in a statement. “By bringing that evidence to the point of care, Vera becomes a trusted clinical intelligence layer, not just another AI tool.”

“New medical knowledge still takes an estimated 17 years to reach clinical practice, according to research in the Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine,” said Taieb Bennani, Vera Health co-founder. “Our mission is to close the gap between what medicine knows and what every patient receives. Today, that gap is measured in years. We want it measured in seconds.”

Bennani told Fierce Healthcare the company’s approach is built around four principles: honesty, traceability, transparency and context.

“The first, and for me the most important, is honesty,” Bennani said. “Language models are built to sound certain; medicine rarely is. A general-purpose model produces plausible sentences, but medicine requires verifiable ones. So we built Vera the other way around: it finds the evidence first, and only then writes the answer. In essence, it’s a search engine that reasons like a clinician.”

The search engine is used by more than 800,000 clinicians in 190 countries, up from “a few thousand” a year ago, Bennani said.

“That growth has been driven by clinicians themselves,” Bennani said. “Most found Vera through another clinician, a colleague down the hall, rather than through a large sales operation. Every month since June, Vera has been the most downloaded clinical app in the world across the App Store and Google Play. In September, it was downloaded more times than several of the biggest players in our space combined, companies worth 100 times or more what we’ve raised.”

Bennani continued, “That’s the clearest sign we’re solving a real problem. Clinicians don’t come back to a tool every day unless it earns their trust. And the need is the same everywhere: across countries, specialties and health systems.”

Vera Health will use the fresh capital to invest further in its evidence infrastructure, international expansion, partnerships and its team, according to Bennani.

“Vera is what it is because of the people who build it, and we love how much a small team can achieve: we doubled from six to 12 people while reaching more than 800,000 clinicians,” Bennani said. “As we grow faster in local markets, we’re now hiring internationally, close to the clinicians and health systems we serve. We’ll grow, but we’ll stay focused and obsessed with the product.”

Vera Health has raised $32 million to date, executives say.

Competition in the clinical AI and medical search market has intensified as established clinical reference companies like Elsevier's ClinicalKey and Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate compete with AI-native tools like OpenEvidence and Doximity Ask, as well as consumer tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic.

news.article_content_zh:
高管表示，Vera Health 的平台扫描了超过 6000 万份同行评审出版物、临床指南等。 (BlackJack3D/GettyImages) 临床人工智能搜索引擎 Vera Health 获得了 2850 万美元的 A 轮融资，以加速和扩展其平台。

Threshold Ventures 领投此轮融资，Optum Ventures、Mantis VC 和 SV Angel 跟投。根据 10 月 27 日的公告，现有投资者 Y Combinator 和 Gradient 在本轮融资中的投资额增加了两倍。

Threshold Ventures 联合创始人兼执行合伙人艾米丽·梅尔顿 (Emily Melton) 在一份声明中表示：“Vera 之所以引人注目，是因为它从证据开始，而不仅仅是答案，帮助临床医生找到和评估决策背后的研究，同时让其优势和局限性显而易见。” “通过将证据带到护理点，Vera 成为值得信赖的临床情报层，而不仅仅是另一个人工智能工具。”

Vera Health 联合创始人 Taieb Bennani 表示：“根据《英国皇家医学会杂志》的研究，新的医学知识估计仍需要 17 年才能达到临床实践。” “我们的使命是缩小医学知识与每位患者接受的知识之间的差距。如今，这种差距以年为单位。我们希望它以秒为单位。”

本纳尼告诉 Fierce Healthcare，该公司的方法是围绕四个原则建立的：诚实、可追溯性、透明度和背景。

“第一，对我来说最重要的是诚实，”本纳尼说。 “语言模型的构建是为了听起来确定；医学很少如此。通用模型会产生看似合理的句子，但医学需要可验证的句子。因此我们以相反的方式构建了 Vera：它首先找到证据，然后才写出答案。本质上，它是一个像临床医生一样进行推理的搜索引擎。”

本纳尼说，该搜索引擎被 190 个国家的超过 80 万名临床医生使用，而一年前只有“几千名”。

“这种增长是由临床医生本身推动的，”本纳尼说。 “大多数人是通过另一位临床医生、大厅里的同事找到 Vera，而不是通过大型销售部门。自 6 月以来，Vera 一直是 App Store 和 Google Play 上全球下载次数最多的临床应用程序。9 月份，它的下载次数比我们领域内几家最大的公司的下载次数总和还多，这些公司的估值是我们筹集的资金的 100 倍甚至更多。”

Bennani 继续说道：“这是我们正在解决实际问题的最明显迹象。临床医生不会每天都使用某种工具，除非它赢得了他们的信任。而且这种需求在任何地方都是一样的：跨国家、跨专业和卫生系统。”

Bennani 表示，Vera Health 将利用新资金进一步投资于其证据基础设施、国际扩张、合作伙伴关系及其团队。

“Vera 之所以能成为现在的样子，是因为它的建造者，我们喜欢小团队所能取得的成就：我们的人数从 6 人增加到 12 人，同时覆盖了超过 800,000 名临床医生，”Bennani 说。 “随着我们在当地市场的增长速度加快，我们现在正在国际上招聘，靠近我们所服务的临床医生和卫生系统。我们会成长，但我们将保持专注和痴迷于产品。”

高管们表示，Vera Health 迄今为止已筹集了 3200 万美元。

随着 Elsevier 的 ClinicalKey 和 Wolters Kluwer 的 UpToDate 等老牌临床参考公司与 OpenEvidence 和 Doximity Ask 等 AI 原生工具以及消费科技巨头 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的竞争，临床 AI 和医学搜索市场的竞争加剧。

news.summary_en: Medical financial AI startup Midstream has raised $20 million in Series A funding led by Valtrius. The company uses AI to help 250 hospitals across the US automate audits and recover revenue from rebates and underpayments from vendors and payers.
news.title_zh: 医疗AI公司Midstream获2000万美元融资
news.summary_zh: 医疗财务AI平台Midstream完成2000万美元A轮融资，旨在解决医院复杂的营收流失与账目纠纷
news.article_content_zh:
Midstream Health通过构建专门针对医疗系统的财务AI模型，深入到医院繁琐的返利协议与多方账目对冲流程中。在现有的医疗支付系统中，因人为审计能力有限，数以十亿计的资金常因账单错误或合同条款执行不到位而产生流失，Midstream的AI正是利用自动化手段填补了这一昂贵的财务黑洞。

本次融资完成后，该公司计划将资金用于扩张团队与技术研发，旨在将其AI审计平台的覆盖范围从现有的250家医院进一步推向全国市场，进一步巩固其在医疗营收周期管理（RCM）领域的竞争壁垒。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 医疗财务AI初创公司Midstream近日完成2000万美元A轮融资，由Valtrius领投。该公司利用AI技术协助全美250家医院自动化审计与追回返利、供应商及支付方的少付账款，通过填补复杂的财务漏洞来直接增加医院营收。

news.title: Broccoli AI, which sells AI agents to plumbing, HVAC, and electrical companies, raised a $22M Series A and a $30M Series B; a source says it is valued at $300M (Nick Lichtenberg/Fortune)
news.title_en: Broccoli AI, which sells AI agents to plumbing, HVAC, and electrical companies, raised a $22M Series A and a $30M Series B; a source says it is valued at $300M (Nick Lichtenberg/Fortune)
news.author: Fortune
news.article_content:
When Marcelle Flowers’ staff told her that two students were waiting at the counter of her Sacramento plumbing shop, she grabbed her wallet. She assumed they were selling chocolate bars for a soccer team.

“I literally said, you have five minutes,” recalled Flowers, now 62 years old. It was June 2024, and a deal to sell her business, Armstrong Plumbing, had fallen through months earlier. She was also “really opposed to AI,” she told Fortune. She feared it would take her people and “take all the jobs.”

The visitors were AJ Jain and Aditya Ketkar, two engineers in their mid-twenties whose energy startup had just fizzled. They had spent that spring walking into about 140 contractors’ shops across Northern California, carrying a diary instead of laptops and offering no sales pitch.

“People were not treating us like salesmen,” Jain said. “Curious kids was, like, our persona,”

They had built exactly one thing worth showing: an automated appointment-reminder call for a San Francisco electrician.

Two years later, their company, Broccoli AI, has raised $52 million across its Series A and Series B. Khosla Ventures led both rounds, with Y Combinator and Operator Partners also participating. The raise was $22 million in Series A and $30 million in Series B, nine months apart, Jain, the company’s cofounder and CEO, told Fortune.

The Series A had not previously been announced. Broccoli is valued at $300 million post-money, according to a person familiar with the matter (Broccoli declined to comment on its valuation). The company had earlier raised $1.5 million in a seed round after going through Y Combinator.

And Marcelle Flowers is now working with the company. She got an apartment in San Francisco to work for them, and her life changed.

“If you had told me that I’d be running an AI company in the heart of San Francisco I would have laughed you out of the room,” Flowers said. “Like, furthest thing from my mind.”

Broccoli sells AI agents to plumbing, HVAC, and electrical companies. They answer inbound calls, book jobs directly into the scheduling software the contractor already uses, follow up on open estimates, and renew service memberships.

The company says more than 1,500 businesses now use it, including Ace Hardware Home Services, Mr. Electric, and Any Hour Group. In the past seven months it has added roofing, pool care, garage doors, home improvement, and exteriors.

Revenue has tripled since the Series A, Jain said, and headcount has grown from 15 people as of 12 months ago to more than 150. The company said the new money will go toward hiring engineers and salespeople as well as speeding up product development.

Owners wanted someone to answer the phone after the office emptied out at 5 p.m., close the books, and chase the estimates technicians wrote up, Jain said. The company says its AI does work equivalent to roughly 30% of a typical contractor’s office staff.

Jain, 27, is the first engineer in a family of business owners on both sides. He and Ketkar met at BITS Pilani in India in 2016 and have been starting companies together since 2017: a delivery app for closed college campuses, an interview-prep boot camp, and, after Y Combinator, a universal API for electric vehicles that took them to London. They signed eight customers there in two years. “We couldn’t scale that business, even after raising a seed round from YC,” Jain said.

They arrived in San Francisco in January 2024. That May and June they went door to door across the Bay Area, then Stockton, Lodi, Modesto, and Sacramento. They wanted an owner to build with.

At the utilities they had worked with before, Jain explained, he used to deal with product managers at 5,000-person companies. A contractor-owner, on the other hand, “cares about solving their customer’s problem.” Owners took them along on smoke breaks and told them how their fathers had started the business.

“The surprising thing is the American Dream is still alive,” Jain said, describing himself and Ketkar as two curious strangers who were met with trust and openness. “No one looked at our accents, our color.”

The turning point was when they met Flowers, who gave them five minutes that changed their lives, Jain said. It was eerie since it almost didn’t happen; Armstrong Plumbing was the only cold call they made twice.

They played her a recording of their one product, an automated call reminding customers of upcoming appointments. Flowers had just lost the employee who made those calls for her shop and hadn’t replaced her. “That hooks me,” she said.

Once the product worked for Flowers, her word of mouth took Broccoli from one customer to 10, and the door-knocking stopped. “She was the operator who helped us create this,” Jain said. “She’s the soul of the company.”

To understand this unlikely alliance, it helps to understand where Flowers came from. Born in 1963, she grew up in a blue-collar family in Anaheim, Calif., one of five children. Her father was a commercial plumber who built restaurants, hotels, and schools, and plumbers were regulars at the family breakfast table, while her mother stayed home. “Very, very much Brady Bunch family,” Flowers said.

She was the middle child and the “hell-raiser.” At 14, she sat her parents down at dinner and told them they were done raising her. “From here on out, I got this,” she recalled saying, describing herself as “barely a high school graduate.” She got pregnant at 19, had her son at 20, and raised him as a single mother. “I really went sideways for a while,” she said. She found her faith at 26.

She has a name for that stretch of life, roughly ages 16 to 26: “the stupid stage.” Decades of hiring young tradesmen gave her patience for men still in it. “I have a lot of grace for people because I was one of those,” she said.

She joined her father’s company in 1995, then opened its residential service-and-repair business in 2011. She said she grew it from about $1 million to $8 million in seven years with no outside capital, operating in a “very male-dominated” field.

COVID hit hard. She said she was sick for about nine months with long COVID, and the business “tanked.” She had already battled cancer twice, she said, both times diagnosed as terminal, and was not expected to live past 35. “I have been through hell and high water in my life,” she said. After she failed to sell the business in 2023, something told her to “wait till June,” and that’s when she met the Broccoli boys. Then a five-minute pitch turned into a half-hour consultation.

Within two days, Flowers recalled, Jain and Ketkar had loaded the reminder bot with her scripts. But her real pain was the answering service. She was paying $5,000 a month for one that booked jobs into her software 33% of the time and asked whether the founders could do for inbound calls what they’d done for outbound. “We had that in 10 days,” she said.

For about three months, Jain said, the founders stopped writing code in San Francisco and began doing it from Flowers’ shop in Sacramento while she explained how a contracting business worked. “They didn’t speak trade,” Flowers said. “They knew nothing about a plunger and a toilet.” She became their first customer, then an adviser, then COO.

Fans of AMC’s Halt and Catch Fire series will recognize the arrangement. In the show, John Bosworth, the Texas computer-company salesman played by Toby Huss, ends up running the business side of a startup founded by a far younger coder: part operator, part surrogate parent. She also designed the logo, the brand colors, and the first trade-show booth. “In my own heart they were like my two kids,” Flowers said of her ostensible bosses. “I didn’t assume the mom role. I probably did a little bit.”

Jain and Flowers both say AI is a teammate rather than a replacement. Jain said a call-center representative at a Utah customer threatened to quit if the owner and his wife took Broccoli away. “It’s not taking away jobs,” Jain said. “It’s making jobs.” Owners who never took vacations now do, he said.

Still, Jain acknowledged limits to what he’s built. The AI is “maybe good at like 80% of the tasks,” he said, with the other 20% needing human judgment. Emergencies such as a flooding basement or a fire go to people in the contractor’s office.

Jain sees Broccoli as a “business in a box” that could let a young technician in, say, Columbus, Ohio, start a company without first hiring a receptionist and a bookkeeper.

By his telling, Broccoli has built maybe 1% of what it plans to, and his company competes with the AI labs “not just for talent, even for real estate,” Jain said. Its San Francisco office shares a parking lot with Cognition, and at least 30% of his engineers still work on-site with customers. Jain said he was in Utah visiting a customer the week before and was headed to Arkansas that Sunday to visit another.

news.article_content_zh:
两位创始人在初创公司失败后，通过走访加州近140家承包商店铺，没有使用PPT演示，而是带着笔记本来倾听需求。他们发现许多蓝领行业经营者在管理预约上极其低效。

news.title: Letter: the White House argues it doesn't have to share the full draft of its voluntary AI testing framework, citing national security and commercial exemptions (Leo Schwartz/The Information)
news.title_en: Letter: the White House argues it doesn't have to share the full draft of its voluntary AI testing framework, citing national security and commercial exemptions (Leo Schwartz/The Information)
news.author: The Information
news.original_content:
Leo Schwartz / The Information:
Letter: the White House argues it doesn't have to share the full draft of its voluntary AI testing framework, citing national security and commercial exemptions  —  The Trump administration declined to produce key documents related
news.content_snippet: The Trump administration declined to produce key documents related to its voluntary AI testing framework …
news.summary_en: In an official response, the White House declined to disclose the complete draft and key records of its voluntary AI testing framework, citing exemptions for national security and confidential commercial information. The administration maintained that withholding the documentation is justified under federal disclosure protections. The move reflects an ongoing effort to introduce voluntary safety standards while shielding tech giants' proprietary algorithms and sensitive defense equities.
news.title_zh: 白宫拒绝公开AI测试框架草案 援引国安与商密豁免
news.summary_zh: 白宫明确拒绝向公众披露自愿性人工智能安全测试框架的完整草案，理由是涉及国家安全和企业商业机密豁免

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 白宫在针对相关记录披露要求的官方回函中，正式拒绝提供其自愿性人工智能测试框架的完整草案及核心文件。官方给出的法律依据是，这批关键记录受到联邦信息披露法中关于国家安全和企业商业机密豁免条款的保护。此举反映出联邦政府在推行AI行业自愿性审查的同时，极力避免强制科技巨头公开底层技术机密或触碰国防敏感信息。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: In an official response, the White House declined to disclose the complete draft and key records of its voluntary AI testing framework, citing exemptions for national security and confidential commercial information. The administration maintained that withholding the documentation is justified under federal disclosure protections. The move reflects an ongoing effort to introduce voluntary safety standards while shielding tech giants' proprietary algorithms and sensitive defense equities.

elements_zh.where: 针对联邦信息公开诉求的官方回函中
elements_zh.what: 拒绝公开自愿性AI安全测试框架的完整草案及关键档案，援引国安与商密豁免
elements_zh.why: 保护合作科技巨头的核心商业利益，并防范前沿AI技术细节泄露带来的潜在国家安全风险

elements_en.where: Official response to federal records disclosure requests
elements_en.what: Refused to produce the full draft and key documents of its voluntary AI testing framework, citing national security and commercial exemptions
elements_en.why: To safeguard corporate proprietary trade secrets and prevent disclosure of sensitive frontier AI capabilities tied to national security

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 所谓“自愿测试”加上“绝密豁免”，翻译成大白话就是：让科技巨头关起门来自己考自己、还不许公众看考卷。既想对外立起“严把AI安全关”的合规牌坊，又舍不得让硅谷金主们受一点委屈，最后“国家安全”再度沦为最好使的万能遮羞布。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Coupling 'voluntary testing' with 'national security exemptions' is classic regulatory theater for letting Big Tech grade its own homework in the dark. It postures as tough on frontier AI safety while ensuring Silicon Valley's corporate secrets remain untouchable behind the ultimate all-purpose shield.

news.title: Hyperbolic, which lets companies rent AI compute across ~30 neoclouds, raised a $30M Series A-1 led by Lip-Bu Tan's Walden Catalyst; it has raised $50M to date (Geoff Weiss/Business Insider)
news.title_en: Hyperbolic, which lets companies rent AI compute across ~30 neoclouds, raised a $30M Series A-1 led by Lip-Bu Tan's Walden Catalyst; it has raised $50M to date (Geoff Weiss/Business Insider)
news.author: Business Insider
news.article_content:
Save Saved As companies scramble for computing power, one challenge is that AI cloud providers, or neoclouds, use a mix of different chips, networking, and software. Hyperbolic helps customers find compute resources from different providers and creates software that makes it easier to use them all, rather than dealing with each one separately.

"It's been a really fragmented market that makes the customer experience really painful," said 31-year-old founder and CEO Jasper Zhang.

Hyperbolic also wants to let customers resell compute that they're paying for but no longer need.

The four-year-old startup works closely with about 30 neoclouds, including WhiteFiber and Vector Core Compute. It says it has roughly $200 million worth of compute connected to its software annually.

Hyperbolic previously raised a $12 million Series A round in 2024, led by Variant and Polychain Capital, following a $7 million seed round earlier that year. The company expects to have 50 employees by the end of the year and will use its funding to expand software tools for managing AI chips across different neoclouds.

Zhang said the company is aiming for $150 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year and is already breaking even. More than 250,000 developers, including teams at Modal, Higgsfield, and Daytona, use Hyperbolic.

Before founding the company, Zhang worked as a quantitative researcher at Citadel Securities. As Wall Street explores ways to financialize AI chips, he said his startup's plans to let companies resell unused compute could help pave the way for a futures market.

Here's a look at the pitch deck Hyperbolic used to raise its $30 million Series A-1. Slides have been redacted so that the deck can be shared publicly.

news.article_content_zh:
随着公司争夺计算能力，人工智能云提供商（或 Neocloud）混合使用不同的芯片、网络和软件，这是一个挑战。双曲线帮助客户找到来自不同提供商的计算资源，并创建软件以更轻松地使用所有资源，而不是单独处理每一项资源。

31 岁的创始人兼首席执行官 Jasper Zhang 表示：“这是一个非常分散的市场，让客户体验非常痛苦。”

Hyperbolic 还希望让客户转售他们已付费但不再需要的计算设备。

这家成立四年的初创公司与大约 30 个 neocloud 密切合作，其中包括 WhiteFiber 和 Vector Core Compute。该公司表示，每年与其软件连接的计算价值约为 2 亿美元。

Hyperbolic 此前在 2024 年筹集了 1200 万美元的 A 轮融资，由 Variant 和 Polychain Capital 领投，此前该轮融资为 700 万美元。该公司预计到今年年底将拥有 50 名员工，并将利用其资金扩展用于跨不同 Neocloud 管理 AI 芯片的软件工具。

张说，公司的目标是到年底实现年度经常性收入 1.5 亿美元，并且已经实现收支平衡。超过 250,000 名开发人员（包括 Modal、Higgsfield 和 Daytona 的团队）使用 Hyperbolic。

在创立公司之前，张先生曾在 Citadel 证券担任量化研究员。在华尔街探索人工智能芯片金融化的方法之际，他表示，他的初创公司计划让公司转售未使用的计算设备，这可能有助于为期货市场铺平道路。

news.title: Saudi Aramco acquires a 49% stake in AI startup Humain, contributing ~$2.6B in cash in 2026 plus AI, compute, and digital assets; Saudi Arabia's PIF retains 51% (Dean Takahashi/GamesBeat)
news.title_en: Saudi Aramco acquires a 49% stake in AI startup Humain, contributing ~$2.6B in cash in 2026 plus AI, compute, and digital assets; Saudi Arabia's PIF retains 51% (Dean Takahashi/GamesBeat)
news.author: GamesBeat
news.article_content:
Saudi Arabia-based oil and energy firm Aramco has acquired a 49% stake in AI firm Humain for $2.6 billion today.

The Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund owns 51% of the Humain, while Aramco now owns 49%$, through a wholly owned subsidiary.

The transaction will further accelerate Humain’s growth and advance its full range of AI capabilities globally, with PIF and Aramco contributing AI assets, capabilities, and talent.

The transaction will accelerate Humain’s ambition to build a globally competitive, integrated AI ecosystem spanning the full stack: from data centers and high-performance compute to advanced models, applications, and industry solutions. Additionally, it will further enable Humain’s plans to develop data center capacity by 2030 and deliver solutions that help the public and private sectors to deploy AI at scale.

The transaction builds on Saudi Arabia’s efforts to further enable the development and deployment of the most advanced data and AI technologies while attracting talent and investment opportunities.

PIF’s strategy for AI and the digital economy benefits from Saudi Arabia’s position as a globally competitive market through innovation and capacity building. Partnering with Aramco in Humain aligns with PIF’s 2026-2030 strategy, which aims to deepen integration across economic ecosystems, expand opportunities with the private sector, and accelerate the growth of national companies into globally competitive leaders.

Aramco is expected to leverage Humain’s AI infrastructure to translate advanced AI capabilities into industrial applications, further enhancing its global ecosystem and operations. Aramco, together with its affiliates, will benefit as a shareholder and strategic partner from HUMAIN’s advanced AI infrastructure and services. With opportunities for revenue growth andattractive margins, this partnership is expected to enhance Aramco’s monetization of existing AI and digital assets, support its broader strategy, and complement its core energy business.

Yazeed A. Al-Humied, Deputy Governor and Head of MENA Investments at PIF, said in a statement: “Bringing PIF and Aramco’s AI portfolio of investments together under Humain creates a powerful synergy that fuels talent growth, technological advancement, and intellectual property creation.”

Al-Humied added, “Fully aligned with PIF’s strategic objectives, this transaction accelerates Humain’s growth into a global leader in the sector, strengthening AI as an enabler of PIF’s six ecosystems and further expanding private sector participation across our portfolio while advancing the development of cutting edge technologies in Saudi Arabia.”

Amin H. Nasser, Aramco president and CEO, said in a statement, “The Humain deal is very important to Aramco, building on the company’s long track record of innovation and technology. We are proud of our achieved progress in developing and deploying advanced digital and AI technologies to enhance performance across the oil and gas sectors.”

Nasser said that since 2023, Aramco has achieved $11.3 billion in Technology Realized Value, with a significant portion coming from AI solutions.

Nasser added, “This partnership with PIF strengthens Aramco’s position as a global technology leader and AI powerhouse, while laying the foundation for localizing the AI industry and enabling faster, more integrated, and scalable deployment of AI systems. AI will therefore play a vital role in the future of business. We are delighted to collaborate with PIF to help shape the future of AI regionally and globally.”

The transaction involves approximately SAR 9.9 billion ($2.6 billion) in cash contributions in 2026 from Aramco to Humain, in addition to AI, compute, and digital assets.

Launched in May 2025, Humain is building full-stack AI capabilities across four core areas: next generation data centers; hyper-performance infrastructure and cloud platforms; advanced AI models including ALLAM, one of the world’s most powerful multimodal Arabic large language models (LLMs); and transformative AI solutions.

Through the deployment of 3 gigawatts of AI data center capacity by 2030, Humain is rapidly scaling to meet growing regional and global demand for AI compute, with the aim of becoming one of the leading exporters of AI globally.

Saudi Arabia-based Aramco is one of the world’s leading integrated energy and chemicals companies, creating value across the hydrocarbon chain and delivering societal and economic benefits to people and communities around the globe. And the Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund (PIF) is one of the world’s largest investors, with a long-term investment strategy to further drive the economic transformation of Saudi Arabia and deliver sustainable financial returns.

news.article_content_zh:
总部位于沙特阿拉伯的石油和能源公司阿美公司今天以 26 亿美元收购了人工智能公司 Humain 49% 的股份。

沙特阿拉伯公共投资基金拥有 Humain 51% 的股份，而沙特阿美公司目前通过全资子公司拥有 49% 的股份。

此次交易将进一步加速 Humain 的增长，并在全球范围内提升其全方位的人工智能能力，PIF 和阿美公司将贡献人工智能资产、能力和人才。

此次交易将加速Humain建立具有全球竞争力的、涵盖全栈的集成人工智能生态系统的雄心：从数据中心和高性能计算到先进模型、应用程序和行业解决方案。此外，它将进一步实现 Humain 到 2030 年开发数据中心容量的计划，并提供帮助公共和私营部门大规模部署人工智能的解决方案。

此次交易建立在沙特阿拉伯努力进一步促进最先进数据和人工智能技术的开发和部署，同时吸引人才和投资机会的基础上。

PIF 的人工智能和数字经济战略受益于沙特阿拉伯通过创新和能力建设作为全球竞争市场的地位。与沙特阿美在 Humain 的合作符合 PIF 的 2026-2030 战略，该战略旨在深化经济生态系统的一体化，扩大与私营部门的机会，并加速国有企业成长为具有全球竞争力的领导者。

沙特阿美预计将利用Humain的人工智能基础设施，将先进的人工智能能力转化为工业应用，进一步增强其全球生态系统和运营。阿美公司及其附属公司将作为股东和战略合作伙伴从 HUMAIN 先进的人工智能基础设施和服务中受益。凭借收入增长的机会和有吸引力的利润率，这一合作伙伴关系预计将增强阿美公司现有人工智能和数字资产的货币化，支持其更广泛的战略，并补充其核心能源业务。

PIF 副行长兼中东和北非投资主管 Yazeed A. Al-Humied 在一份声明中表示：“将 PIF 和阿美石油公司的人工智能投资组合纳入 Humain 旗下，可产生强大的协同效应，推动人才增长、技术进步和知识产权创造。”

Al-Humied 补充道：“此次交易完全符合 PIF 的战略目标，加速 Humain 成长为该行业的全球领导者，加强人工智能作为 PIF 六个生态系统推动者的地位，并进一步扩大私营部门在我们投资组合中的参与，同时推动沙特阿拉伯尖端技术的发展。”

沙特阿美总裁兼首席执行官阿明·H·纳赛尔 (Amin H. Nasser) 在一份声明中表示：“Humain 交易对沙特阿美来说非常重要，它建立在公司长期创新和技术记录的基础上。我们为我们在开发和部署先进数字和人工智能技术以提高石油和天然气行业绩效方面取得的进展感到自豪。”

纳赛尔表示，自 2023 年以来，阿美公司已实现 113 亿美元的技术实现价值，其中很大一部分来自人工智能解决方案。

Nasser 补充道：“与 PIF 的合作巩固了阿美公司作为全球技术领导者和人工智能强国的地位，同时为人工智能行业本地化以及实现更快、更集成和可扩展的人工智能系统部署奠定了基础。因此，人工智能将在未来的商业中发挥至关重要的作用。我们很高兴与 PIF 合作，帮助塑造区域和全球人工智能的未来。”

除了人工智能、计算和数字资产之外，该交易还涉及阿美公司在 2026 年向 Humain 提供约 99 亿沙特里亚尔（26 亿美元）的现金捐助。

Humain 于 2025 年 5 月推出，正在构建跨四个核心领域的全栈人工智能功能：下一代数据中心；超高性能基础设施和云平台；先进的人工智能模型，包括 ALLAM，世界上最强大的多模式阿拉伯语大语言模型 (LLM) 之一；和变革性的人工智能解决方案。

通过到 2030 年部署 3 吉瓦的人工智能数据中心容量，Humain 正在快速扩展，以满足区域和全球对人工智能计算不断增长的需求，目标是成为全球领先的人工智能出口商之一。

总部位于沙特阿拉伯的阿美公司是世界领先的综合能源和化学品公司之一，在整个碳氢化合物链上创造价值，并为全球人民和社区带来社会和经济效益。沙特阿拉伯公共投资基金（PIF）是全球最大的投资者之一，其长期投资战略旨在进一步推动沙特阿拉伯的经济转型并带来可持续的财务回报。
