If the file cannot be fetched (the page opened as a file), the stays. --> Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights Authors Rikiya Takehi*

We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.

In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.

We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.

For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.

It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.

Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.

We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.

Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.

Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.

We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.

We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.

The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along (Figure 1). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python.

Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.

So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.

We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck.

We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights.

From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest.

Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot.

We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network.

Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest.

How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.

So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space.

From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space.

We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access.

Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes.

We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes.

With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games.

How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more.

Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly.

We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA datasetThe QA dataset: GitHub.. One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning.

Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained.

It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion (Figure 2).

Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights.

We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed.

As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights.

With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining.

Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem.

Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly.

Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them .

On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools.

In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization.

This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples:

We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline.

We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number.

Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty, Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab, Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations!

Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project.

If the file cannot be fetched (the page opened as a file), the stays. --> Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights Authors Rikiya Takehi*

We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.

In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.

We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.

For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.

It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.

Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.

We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.

Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.

Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.

We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.

We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.

The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along (Figure 1). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python.

Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.

So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.

We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck.

We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights.

From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest.

Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot.

We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network.

Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest.

How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.

So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space.

From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space.

We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access.

Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes.

We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes.

With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games.

How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more.

Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly.

We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA datasetThe QA dataset: GitHub.. One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning.

Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained.

It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion (Figure 2).

Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights.

We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed.

As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights.

With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining.

Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem.

Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly.

Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them .

On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools.

In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization.

This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples:

We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline.

We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number.

Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty, Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab, Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations!

Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project.

它位于源 --> 中，SVG 无法使用页面的 Web 字体并回退到 Helvetica，因此每个字体都会放入页面本身：然后将其文本设置为 Source Sans 3 和 JetBrains Mono，就像其他字体一样。如果无法获取文件（页面作为文件打开），则保留。 --> 权重空间编程的火花：法学硕士可以原生读写神经网络权重 作者 Rikiya Takehi*

我们发现前沿法学硕士在本机读取和编写神经网络权重方面出人意料地出色，远远超出了我们对人类或传统算法的期望。这对于优化和可解释性来说可能都是一件大事。

只需查看原始权重，GPT-6 Astra 就可以判断网络经过训练要做什么。在没有任何环境反馈的情况下，它可以轻松地从头开始编写小型游戏网络，其性能超过使用 PPO 训练的网络 1 亿步。

同样，当被要求在没有梯度的情况下让 Qwen3.5-0.8B 更好地进行数学计算时，Astra 发现了其权重中的一个问题，导致 Qwen 自己的模型卡警告的推理循环，并通过本地编辑 0.016% 的权重来修复此问题。在相同的采样设置下，这种权重校正将 MATH-500 从 7.9% 提高到 48.1%，并且开箱即用地推广到指令遵循，将 IFEval 提高了 3 倍。

所有这一切都是可能的，而无需允许 Astra 编写训练循环。它利用推理来找出神经网络的每个部分计算或应该计算什么，并相应地改变权重。我们称之为权重空间规划。

纵观深度学习的历史，我们将简单的归纳偏差编码为 Adam 或 Muon 等微小的符号优化器。这种情况正在发生变化：我们的神经网络权重很快就会由法学硕士进行本地优化，这些法学硕士会刻意推理其权重。

如果你被要求手工制作一个下围棋的神经网络，你会做什么？如果给你原始的神经网络权重并要求你预测它们的行为，你会从哪里开始呢？对于几乎任何人来说，这实际上是不可能的。

如今，权重是通过优化、通过训练来编写权重的自定义网络或通过正式程序的编译器来编写的。在这篇文章中，我们发现当前一代在自然语言中使用的前沿法学硕士开始变得异常擅长理解和围绕自然语言目标构建神经网络权重。

几年来，我们一直在使用法学硕士来优化文本工件，例如提示和围绕它们构建的程序。最近，我们开始使用它们来优化整个工具以及训练 ML 模型的训练代码和超参数。

我们经常通过以下事实来证明这些方法的合理性：我们不知道其他原则性的方法来爬山文本工件，这与更新可微神经网络的权重不同。毕竟，人类可以手动“优化”代码，因此要求法学硕士这样做是有意义的，但他们无法手动“优化”神经权重，因此这些很大程度上仍停留在符号算法领域。

在这篇文章中，我们分享了非常早期的结果，这些结果使我们能够论证推理驱动优化的范式现在甚至对于可微神经网络来说也即将到来。

在权重空间编程中，通用 LLM 围绕某些自然语言规范直接读取和写入网络的权重（即不通过优化器，特别是不使用梯度下降），有时甚至根本没有环境反馈。

在自然语言中，“只需要求”法学硕士就可以在神经网络的权重中找到隐藏的特征或故障，修复该故障，或者从头开始编写一个新网络。我们报告了以下各项的早期令人兴奋的结果，首先是在小型网络上，然后甚至是在真实的语言模型上：

我们从一个小规模的实验开始，看看法学硕士是否可以理解连续权重空间，它本质上只是一个数字列表。

items.title: Memo: Linux distribution vendor SUSE is laying off ~10% of its staff, saying "automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate" (Liam Proven/The Register)
items.title_en: Memo: Linux distribution vendor SUSE is laying off ~10% of its staff, saying "automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate" (Liam Proven/The Register)
items.author: The Register
items.article_content:
One in ten employees at SUSE are facing the chop due to "automation and AI," according to a memo dispatched by management at the privately owned open source software biz.

In an email to the 1,900 strong workforce on Monday - seen by The Register - CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen, the former Red Hat exec who joined SUSE in March 2023, confirmed the "difficult news."

"We are announcing a reduction of SUSE’s global workforce of approximately 10 percent," he said. "These decisions are painful for our people, our culture, and our open source community, but they are necessary for us to adapt and build a sustainable, resilient SUSE for the long term."

Van Leeuwen says the business, bought by Swedish private equity provider EQT, decided to cut jobs after scrutinizing its "future strategy, required capabilities, and team structures." The rest of the organization will get a look at the fiscal year 2027 strategy on November 16.

"What is clear is that automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate. AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work. We have seen this trend already both inside our sector and in the wider economy. This means that the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.

"We are adapting. Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years. This means we are accelerating investments in high priority areas, and deprioritizing others. These are hard, painful decisions to make, but necessary for our future."

As The Reg reported in 2025, SUSE doubled down on AI.

The specific roles at risk of redundancy were not outlined but SUSE claims it has considered where the people in those positions are "able to evolve, what they can stop doing, what they need to do more of - and decisions have been made on that basis."

Staff caught up in the redundancies will be informed by November 4, employee representatives nominated the following day, and one to one meetings will begin at the start of next week.

Van Leeuwen says in the internal memo that the job cuts are a "reflection of shifting organizational needs, not your talent or commitment. You have tackled hard infrastructure and open source challenges that power critical enterprise systems around the world.

"Any organization will be fortunate to have your expertise."

Back in September, we reported that the company was asking old hands if they would take "voluntary separation." It seems not enough people chose to walk through the door, so instead, they're getting thrown through it instead. SUSE "geckos" in the Czech Republic may be glad they joined a trade union.

Back in 2018, EQT bought SUSE from Microfocus for $2.5 billion. EQT floated SUSE on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in 2021 with slightly disappointing results. A couple of years later, new CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen took over, and later in 2023, EQT chose to take the company private again.

The commercial context is that in March SUSE's corporate owner EQT was reportedly considering selling it off again. ®

items.article_content_zh:
根据这家私营开源软件公司管理层发布的一份备忘录，SUSE 十分之一的员工因“自动化和人工智能”而面临裁员。

The Register 看到，2023 年 3 月加入 SUSE 的前红帽高管、首席执行官 Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen 在周一发给 1,900 名员工的电子邮件中证实了这一“艰难的消息”。

“我们宣布 SUSE 全球员工人数减少约 10%，”他说。 “这些决定对我们的人民、我们的文化和我们的开源社区来说都是痛苦的，但对于我们适应和建立长期可持续、有弹性的 SUSE 来说，它们是必要的。”

Van Leeuwen 表示，该公司被瑞典私募股权提供商 EQT 收购，在仔细审查其“未来战略、所需能力和团队结构”后决定裁员。该组织的其他成员将于 11 月 16 日了解 2027 财年战略。

“显而易见的是，自动化和人工智能正在从根本上改变软件公司的运营方式。人工智能能力正在呈指数级增长，迫使我们从根本上重新构想我们的工作。我们已经在我们的行业内部和更广泛的经济中看到了这种趋势。这意味着 SUSE 所建立的组织设计和成本基础将无法推动我们成功前进。

“我们正在适应。在 SUSE 中，现代工具已经改变了我们的日常工作流程，使团队能够以更少的运营开销和更扁平的报告关系更快地行动。对某些现有角色的要求已大大减少。其他角色将在未来几年内发展。这意味着我们正在加速对高优先领域的投资，并降低其他领域的优先级。这些都是艰难而痛苦的决定，但对我们的未来来说是必要的。”

正如 The Reg 在 2025 年报道的那样，SUSE 在人工智能方面加倍努力。

没有概述面临裁员风险的具体角色，但 SUSE 声称它已经考虑了这些职位的人员“能够在哪些方面发展，他们可以停止做什么，他们需要做更多的事情 - 并在此基础上做出了决定。”

陷入裁员的员工将于 11 月 4 日之前收到通知，第二天提名员工代表，一对一会议将于下周初开始。

Van Leeuwen 在内部备忘录中表示，裁员是“组织需求变化的反映，而不是你的才能或承诺。你已经解决了为全球关键企业系统提供动力的硬基础设施和开源挑战。

“任何组织都会很幸运拥有您的专业知识。”

早在九月，我们就报道过该公司正在询问老员工是否愿意“自愿离职”。似乎没有足够多的人选择走进这扇门，所以相反，他们被扔了进去。捷克共和国的 SUSE“壁虎”可能很高兴他们加入了工会。

早在 2018 年，EQT 以 25 亿美元从 Microfocus 手中收购了 SUSE。 EQT 于 2021 年在法兰克福证券交易所上市 SUSE，但结果略显令人失望。几年后，新任首席执行官 Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen 接任，并于 2023 年晚些时候，EQT 选择再次将公司私有化。

商业背景是，3 月份，据报道 SUSE 的企业所有者 EQT 正在考虑再次出售它。 ®

items.title: SpaceXSI apparently cuts Grok Bot quotas weeks after Musk called it his fastest-growing product
items.title_en: SpaceXSI apparently cuts Grok Bot quotas weeks after Musk called it his fastest-growing product
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
SpaceXSI is apparently cutting usage limits for its AI agent Grok Bot, less than two weeks after Musk called it his fastest-growing product. The operating costs were "unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on X. OpenAI and Anthropic are also tightening their flat-rate plans as they grapple with the high costs of AI agents.

The article SpaceXSI apparently cuts Grok Bot quotas weeks after Musk called it his fastest-growing product appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: Anthropic confirms new Claude Code limits "to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game", saying IP infringement violates its usage policy (Bruno Ferreira/Tom's Hardware)
items.title_en: Anthropic confirms new Claude Code limits "to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game", saying IP infringement violates its usage policy (Bruno Ferreira/Tom's Hardware)
items.author: Tom's Hardware
items.article_content:
Meanwhile, we now have direct reports of reverse engineering efforts being blocked, while online complaints grow.

In the full tweet, which you can read below, Addy Osmani says that "[Anthropic] added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against [its] usage policy." He goes on to state that work on original games is meant to continue working, and that Anthropic is iterating on the rules to try and "strike the right balance."

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way.October 30, 2026

There's no telling what those sentences might be, though given Osmani's choice of words, it's possible that said sentences are indeed what X user Chasm posted a screenshot of: "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."

In our previous report, we had already linked to recent issues raised at Claude Code's own GitHub repository, comprised of users complaining that the AI assistant was refusing to work on their games or on reverse-engineering tasks. As far as we can ascertain, it appears the game-related blocking is limited to the combination of using Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model. Should that prove true, then users should be able to sidestep the limitation by calling upon Opus using another harness like Ollama or forwarding specific requests through a wrapper of some sort.

Regarding the blocking of reverse engineering, we have received direct confirmations. The first comes from our own alumnus Jarred Walton, who was trying to run checks on the software he's developing. He notes that such work had been performed with no issue until yesterday, October 31, and that switching to Opus 4.8 let him continue his work.

Walton theorizes that Anthropic may have added a new rule to Code specifically for reverse-engineering. Considering that timing, plus the fact that other reports of refusals all popped up around the last week, may indicate that the company could be fiddling with cybersecurity-related rules in the same manner as they are for video game-related content.

We also received screenshots from a staffer's direct acquaintance, who asked Opus 5.5 (via Code) to try and reverse engineer a product activation, a request that likewise triggered safeguards. Meanwhile, notices that Claude Code appears to block reverse-engineering continue to mount, now with a Redditor allegedly having their account suspended, and then reinstated, over using Opus 5.5 and Reverse Engineer Anything. The company has an ongoing Cyber Verification Program, in which only approved entities get access to the full set of frontier models' cybersecurity capabilities.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

Meanwhile, notices that Claude Code appears to block reverse-engineering continue to mount, now with a Redditor allegedly having their account suspended, and then reinstated, over using Opus 5.5 and Reverse Engineer Anything. The company has an ongoing Cyber Verification Program, in which only approved entities get access to the full set of frontier models' cybersecurity capabilities.

items.article_content_zh:
与此同时，我们现在收到了有关逆向工程工作被阻止的直接报告，而网上投诉也在增加。

在完整的推文中（您可以在下面阅读），Addy Osmani 表示“[Anthropic] 在 Opus 5.5 上的 Claude Code 提示中添加了两句话，以引导其远离重新创建其他人的特定游戏，因为使用 Claude 侵犯知识产权违反了[其]使用政策。”他接着表示，原创游戏的工作应该继续进行，Anthropic 正在迭代规则，试图“达到适当的平衡”。

我们在 Opus 5.5 上的 Claude Code 提示中添加了两句话，以阻止其重新创建其他人的特定游戏，因为使用 Claude 侵犯知识产权违反了我们的使用政策。原创游戏、类型游戏以及根据您自己的设计和资产构建的游戏旨在继续发挥作用。我们将继续迭代以确保我们取得正确的平衡。与此同时，如果克劳德拒绝了属于你的东西，请将其发送给我。2026 年 10 月 30 日

目前还不清楚这些句子可能是什么，但考虑到 Osmani 的用词选择，这些句子可能确实是 X 用户 Chasm 发布的屏幕截图：“要构建原创游戏、某种类型的游戏以及根据用户自己的设计和资产构建的游戏。不要构建特定现有游戏的娱乐版，即使它被重命名或称为原创。”

在我们之前的报告中，我们已经链接到了 Claude Code 自己的 GitHub 存储库中最近提出的问题，其中包括用户抱怨人工智能助手拒绝处理他们的游戏或逆向工程任务。据我们所知，与游戏相关的阻塞似乎仅限于使用 Claude Code 和 Opus 5.5 模型的组合。如果这一点被证明是正确的，那么用户应该能够通过使用 Ollama 等其他工具调用 Opus 或通过某种包装器转发特定请求来避开限制。

关于逆向工程的封锁，我们已经收到了直接确认。第一个来自我们的校友贾里德·沃尔顿（Jarred Walton），他试图对他正在开发的软件进行检查。他指出，直到昨天 10 月 31 日，此类工作都没有出现任何问题，而切换到 Opus 4.8 让他可以继续工作。

沃尔顿推测，人类可能在代码中添加了一条专门用于逆向工程的新规则。考虑到这个时间点，再加上上周出现的其他拒绝报告的事实，可能表明该公司可能会以与视频游戏相关内容相同的方式摆弄网络安全相关规则。

我们还收到了一名员工的熟人发来的屏幕截图，他要求 Opus 5.5（通过代码）尝试对产品激活进行逆向工程，这一请求同样触发了安全措施。与此同时，注意到 Claude Code 似乎阻止逆向工程继续增加，据称现在有一名 Redditor 的帐户因使用 Opus 5.5 和逆向工程 Anything 而被暂停，然后又恢复。该公司有一个持续的网络验证计划，只有获得批准的实体才能访问全套前沿模型的网络安全功能。

items.title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
items.title_en: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.

Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.

Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.

在本报告调查的组织中，只有不到一半的代理生成的见解能够带来业务改进。尽管大多数受访者称赞其代理的描述性见解的质量，但对他们的规范性见解（行动所依据的见解）的评论显然是褒贬不一。

如果无法产生改善业务的见解，组织就会无法获得代理分析所需的投资回报。更糟糕的是，有缺陷的见解会引发错误的行动，可能会导致声誉或财务损失。该报告衡量了公司如何看待其分析代理产生的输出质量，并探讨了组织如何寻求提高洞察质量并让其代理为业务更加努力地工作。

items.title: Israeli startup 42AI, which is developing a "behavioral world model" that tries to predict human behavior, emerges from stealth with a $62.5M seed (Ram Iyer/TechCrunch)
items.title_en: Israeli startup 42AI, which is developing a "behavioral world model" that tries to predict human behavior, emerges from stealth with a $62.5M seed (Ram Iyer/TechCrunch)
items.author: TechCrunch
items.article_content:
Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?

Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions.

“Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.

“A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision.

42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.

“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added CTO and co-founder Ehud Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”

“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.

The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions).

Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured.

42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said.

In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity.

In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly.

He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events).

And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague.

Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.

Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging.

The $62.5 million seed funding came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years, and wasn’t entirely raised from external investors, Gal-Or said. Infinity was founded by his father, Amir Gal-Or, who is also 42AI’s chairman and a co-founder. 42AI now plans to raise more money.

Beyond finance, 42AI is now exploring applications for its model in gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity, and one day wants to use it to help robots and AI agents understand people. But that may be a ways off yet: Ezra acknowledged that the model needs to be trained on rules and context for each new domain.

And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: if a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? Ezra admitted that this was “a valid concern” when I raised it, and the founders pointed to regulations, monitoring and an internal ethics committee, though they didn’t explain what, if anything, would stop their customers from using the technology to gain an advantage over the very people it’s profiling.

Gal-Or, however, was confident that the technology could help address such risks. “We are very proud that actually we are part of the solution; we are the solution to this problem,” he said.

42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.

“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added CTO and co-founder Ehud Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”

“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.

The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions).

Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured.

42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said.

In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity.

In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly.

He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events).

And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague.

Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.

Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging.

The $62.5 million seed funding came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years, and wasn’t entirely raised from external investors, Gal-Or said. Infinity was founded by his father, Amir Gal-Or, who is also 42AI’s chairman and a co-founder. 42AI now plans to raise more money.

Beyond finance, 42AI is now exploring applications for its model in gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity, and one day wants to use it to help robots and AI agents understand people. But that may be a ways off yet: Ezra acknowledged that the model needs to be trained on rules and context for each new domain.

And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: if a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? Ezra admitted that this was “a valid concern” when I raised it, and the founders pointed to regulations, monitoring and an internal ethics committee, though they didn’t explain what, if anything, would stop their customers from using the technology to gain an advantage over the very people it’s profiling.

Gal-Or, however, was confident that the technology could help address such risks. “We are very proud that actually we are part of the solution; we are the solution to this problem,” he said.

items.article_content_zh:
这是一个直接来自科幻小说的问题：如果人工智能能够在你决定做什么之前预测你将要做什么，即使是在一个全新的情况下，会怎么样？

以色列初创公司 42AI 表示，它正在开发一种可以做到这一点的“行为世界模型”，并且刚刚获得 6250 万美元的种子资金。该公司最初在少数金融经纪公司运行其预测系统，该公司表示该模型可以帮助预测个体交易者将如何应对波动的情况。

当我请 42AI 的首席执行官兼联合创始人 Amit Gal-Or 证明其公司的高调说法时，他告诉 TechCrunch：“行为不是确定性的；它始终是概率性的。”他认为，即使环境发生变化，人们也有潜在的心理倾向，这些倾向会影响他们的决定，而这正是初创公司试图测量的内容，并将其转换为模型可以理解的数据。

他的联合创始人兼首席技术官埃胡德·埃兹拉 (Ehud Ezra) 补充道：“一周后，你可能会变成另一个人，但你的倾向总会在某些领域以概率或分布的方式发挥作用。”该公司认为，这就是该模型的作用：显示一个人做出某个决定的概率。

42AI 表示，该模型试图找出人们的内部动机，而不是根据人们之前的行为推断模式。为此，42AI 研究了人们对看似无关的事件的反应。例如，对于投资者或交易者来说，此类事件可能包括完成 KYC 流程、入职、支持电话、转账或股票交易。

“当人们在初始流程中与支持人员或销售人员交谈时 [...]，我们会关注情绪、声音、他们正在进行的大量互动、他们打电话的次数等等，”首席技术官兼联合创始人 Ehud Ezra 补充道。 “所有这些数据点都将进入模型。稍后，您将进行交互：如何买卖以及何时买卖，我们正在关注该阶段的市场。”

“所以我们试图了解他们如何看待世界。在世界模型中，每个人都是世界，”他补充道。

然后，该公司将这些观察结果转换为特征的数学表示，然后将其输入到基于变压器的世界模型中，该模型列出了在不同情况下可能做出的决策的概率。 （该公司使用单独的语言模型来为其预测生成解释）。

埃兹拉说，该模型经过训练，可以在模拟过程中保留一个人的潜在倾向。因此，如果某人通常厌恶风险，但模型突然将他们视为冒险者，那么“目标就偏离了”，他解释了模型的训练奖励是如何构建的。

42AI 花了三年时间开发这种方法，将心理学研究与神经科学和遗传学相结合，并听取了心理学和创伤后应激障碍 (PTSD) 专家以及 2011 年诺贝尔化学奖获得者丹·谢赫特曼 (Dan Shechtman) 的建议。

Gal-Or 表示，该团队首先通过心理评估和行为场景研究了数千人，然后添加了覆盖超过 200 万人的政府和生物银行数据集。他说，其客户数据集已扩大到覆盖近 3000 万人。

在实时部署中，该模型分析客户的现有记录，包括交易和支持电话。 Gal-Or 指出该系统不需要个人身份信息，并认为“模型永远不知道这个人是谁。”然而，该公司似乎仍然根据链接的客户活动创建个人行为档案。

在预测市场交易方面，42AI 声称其模型的准确率达到 98%，但 Gal-Or 澄清说，这更多的是衡量交易流量是否落在预测范围内，而不是衡量每笔交易是否预测正确。

他还表示，该模型在预测交易方向和交易量方面始终达到 0.8 至 0.85 的 F1 分数。 （F1 分数是机器学习中的一个指标，用于衡量分类模型在正确预测与误报和错过事件之间的平衡程度）。

items.title: Amended S-1: Anthropic says it has purchase commitments and lease agreements of $895.4B, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure" (Ashley Capoot/CNBC)
items.title_en: Amended S-1: Anthropic says it has purchase commitments and lease agreements of $895.4B, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure" (Ashley Capoot/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.

The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.

Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering. The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.

During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.

The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.

As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds, and quarterly reports from Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.

The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.

In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."

Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.

"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.

The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut.

Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives.

"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.

items.article_content_zh:
Anthropic 周一在向美国证券交易委员会提交的修订后的 S-1 表格中报告了最新的财务状况，让投资者能够更全面地了解其业务状况。

这家人工智能公司表示，截至 9 月 30 日的 9 个月内，其收入为 332.4 亿美元，比去年同期增长约 1,200%。该公司报告期内净亏损 1,040 亿美元，但其中大部分是由于可转换票据和衍生负债公允价值的变化造成的。 2025 年同期，Anthropic 亏损 251 亿美元。

Anthropic 上周公布了备受期待的招股说明书，使该公司距离潜在的历史性首次公开募股又近了一步。最初的文件仅包括克劳德制造商今年上半年的财务状况。

Anthropic 第三季度的收入约为 170 亿美元，比去年同期增长约 1,127%。然而，收入增长逐季放缓。第三季度收入增长约 47%，较第二季度的 144% 和第一季度的 132% 增幅大幅下降。

该公司第三季度净亏损 232.9 亿美元。

当这家成立 5 年的公司准备开始路演时，它将不得不面对围绕人工智能建设日益增长的市场不安情绪。华尔街一直担心利率上升将使许多数据中心开发商和neoclouds无力承担债务，而微软、Alphabet和亚马逊上周发布的季度报告加剧了这些担忧。

超大规模企业积极的人工智能支出正在蚕食他们的现金流，导致一些投资者担心计算能力可能无法足够快地上线以满足 Anthropic 的需求。 Anthropic 的大部分容量来自亚马逊、谷歌和 SpaceX，但它也依赖 Neoclouds 进行一些计算，因为它正在竞相尽快扩张。

在修订后的 S-1 中，Anthropic 表示已签订采购承诺和租赁协议，承诺支出总额约为 8954 亿美元，“基本上所有支出都与计算和基础设施有关”。

Anthropic 表示，截至 9 月 30 日的 9 个月，其计算和基础设施支出增加了 144 亿美元，较去年同期增长 329%。

Anthropic 在文件中表示：“随着我们的计算和基础设施容量的增长，相关的计算和基础设施费用也随之增加。”

该公司的首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代 (Dario Amodei) 与其他几位从目前其主要竞争对手 OpenAI 叛逃的研究人员共同创立了 Anthropic。 OpenAI 于 6 月向 SEC 秘密提交了招股说明书，但其高管已表示其目标是在 2027 年首次亮相。

Anthropic 致力于将自己定位为比竞争对手更具安全意识的品牌，其 S-1 包含 90 多页的风险因素。该公司强调了风险，包括潜在的政治阻力、复杂的基础设施需求以及平衡安全和商业目标可能带来的困难。

Anthropic 的联合创始人在文件中表示：“我们认为，我们个人有责任帮助世界了解这些风险，在我们的人工智能模型中预防或减轻这些风险，并与政府和行业其他部门合作，在社会层面解决这些风险。”

items.title: Anthropic grows revenue twelvefold but posts $23 billion loss
items.title_en: Anthropic grows revenue twelvefold but posts $23 billion loss
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Anthropic swings back to an operating loss ahead of its blockbuster IPO. According to Bloomberg, the company posted quarterly revenue of nearly $17 billion, twelve times what it brought in a year earlier. But operating costs of $17.5 billion outpaced that revenue, wiping out the profit Anthropic had reported the previous quarter, according to The Information. The net loss came in at $23.3 billion for the quarter, up from $12.1 billion a year ago.

Anthropic pointed to two main drivers behind the cost spike: $5 billion for short-term compute capacity it locked in and $2 billion in employee donation matching. The company has been grappling with a compute crunch since late last year. According to the New York Times, it has since signed dozens of deals with Amazon, Google, SpaceX, chipmakers, and former crypto miners. Anthropic is expected to have access to more than 3.5 gigawatts of power this year and plans to double that next year.

All told, the company's updated prospectus shows $895 billion in commitments for compute and data center leases. Those costs add pressure on the IPO, which could raise around $100 billion, the New York Times reports. Up to $3.5 billion of that is expected to come from Japanese investors.

在轰动一时的 IPO 之前，Anthropic 再次陷入运营亏损。据彭博社报道，该公司公布的季度收入接近 170 亿美元，是上年同期的 12 倍。但据 The Information 报道，175 亿美元的运营成本超过了收入，抹去了 Anthropic 上一季度报告的利润。该季度净亏损为 233 亿美元，高于去年同期的 121 亿美元。

Anthropic 指出成本飙升背后的两个主要驱动因素：锁定的 50 亿美元短期计算能力和 20 亿美元的员工捐赠匹配。自去年年底以来，该公司一直在努力应对计算危机。据《纽约时报》报道，此后该公司已与亚马逊、谷歌、SpaceX、芯片制造商和前加密货币矿工签署了数十项协议。 Anthropic 预计今年将获得超过 3.5 吉瓦的电力，并计划明年将这一数字增加一倍。

总而言之，该公司更新后的招股说明书显示，其计算和数据中心租赁承诺金额为 8950 亿美元。据《纽约时报》报道，这些成本增加了 IPO 的压力，IPO 可能筹集约 1000 亿美元资金。其中高达 35 亿美元预计将来自日本投资者。

items.title: A profile of OpenAI VP Charles Porch, an ex-Instagram executive who is rehabilitating AI's image across Hollywood and the media, including via celebrity dinners (Charlotte Klein/New York Magazine)
items.title_en: A profile of OpenAI VP Charles Porch, an ex-Instagram executive who is rehabilitating AI's image across Hollywood and the media, including via celebrity dinners (Charlotte Klein/New York Magazine)
items.author: New York Magazine
items.article_content:
Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section.

Photo: Danielle Levitt for New York Magazine Photo: Danielle Levitt for New York Magazine In August, news leaked that Gwyneth Paltrow was set to host “a private, off-the-record, alfresco dinner” at her Amagansett home in honor of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “I guess summers in the Hamptons just aren’t complete these days without sucking up to our new AI overlords,” Puck’s Matt Belloni, who broke the news, wrote. “Luckily, Gwyneth Paltrow has you covered.” The backlash was vicious — “tone-deaf dumbass,” one X user wrote — and the dinner was postponed.

“God, the internet made it such a bigger thing than it was,” says Charles Porch, who brokered the dinner with Paltrow’s team, as he sips an Arnold Palmer on a crisp afternoon in October outside Sant Ambroeus in Soho. “Gwyneth invests in the space. She does these investor dinners all the time. Sam was coming through town and I was like, ‘Let’s just do this.’”

Altman had hired Porch in 2025 to do for OpenAI what he had done so successfully for Instagram for more than a decade: persuade famous people in Hollywood and beyond to use and partner with the platform and help the tech company be culturally relevant. The freak-out over Paltrow’s dinner reflected how much public sentiment toward big tech had shifted since Porch’s Instagram days, when Anna Wintour hosted the same kind of event for its CEO at the time, Kevin Systrom. I ask him if it made him rethink the playbook. “It makes it look like that’s the strategy, and it’s not the strategy. That was, like, a dinner,” Porch says. “But I know those dinners are effective because I see it. We did the dinner eventually, and it was great.” It took place at the apartment of an AI enthusiast at the end of September in New York.

Everyone above a certain income bracket seems to know Charles Porch, but few can tell you what exactly he does. He showed up in Los Angeles in his grandmother’s Honda Accord wagon when he was 20 and spent the next two decades cultivating a formidable network of celebrities and influencers. “He took one step at a time very carefully, never burned a single bridge, never spoke out of turn, never took advantage of an opportunity in the wrong way,” says Erin Foster, the well-connected daughter of music producer David Foster, who met Porch when they were both underlings at Warner Bros. Records.

“I’m not a business-development guy or the brand guy. I’m the relationships person that’s bringing everyone along on new tech,” says Porch, 45, a self-described “tech optimist” who has long been comfortable in the gray area between the personal and the professional. “There’s a strategy around making friends.”

When he arrived in New York just before the pandemic, few seemed to notice. For those who either didn’t know or didn’t care about what was going on in Menlo Park in the early 2010s, the first time they heard of Porch was likely after his wedding to the billionaire’s scion Robert Denning in 2025, three days of Parisian opulence shared with Jerry and Jessica Seinfeld, Mariska Hargitay, Antony Blinken, Harry Styles (with whom he shares a godchild), Nicky Hilton Rothschild, Darren Walker, Jenna Lyons, and various European aristocrats. After that of Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos, it turned out to be the ritziest wedding of the summer. Suddenly, he and Denning were everywhere, a power-gay couple imbuing the fabric of New York society, at every gala and fundraiser and opening. The swirl of Porch’s life plays out on his Instagram Stories: courtside at the Knicks’ season opener, Hawaii for Jen Meyer’s star-studded wedding, Paris to see Céline Dion with Reese Witherspoon and Karlie Kloss.

In the process of connecting entertainment and tech, he has found himself at the center of several overlapping circles of power — and become a character in his own right. “I know, scary,” he says when I point this out. “He is really good at putting a room together, and now he is of the room,” says someone who worked with him. “He was someone who understood the room before he was part of the Establishment.”

It’s not hard to see why OpenAI would want Porch on its side. “It’s funny: I think everyone wants to hate Open AI and everyone wants to love Charles Porch,” says podcaster Nayeema Raza. “That’s probably the value for Sam.”

Porch’s job was never going to be easy. Why would artists and other creative types want to plug something that threatens to replace them? “The full-throated endorsement of AI is probably the biggest third-rail issue in Hollywood right now. And people are terrified,” says a media executive. Headlines about AI in recent months have generated panic about not just job displacement and copyright infringement but also OpenAI agents going rogue and threatening to take down the entire internet. The evil of the tech industry is the subject of several of the year’s biggest films — made by precisely the industry Porch is trying to court. “Charles can get them to sit down and listen to Sam Altman lay out his vision. But if the vision is ‘I’m going to destroy your industry,’ it doesn’t really matter,” says one of Porch’s former colleagues.

“I’m trying to pinpoint ways and moments where AI can show up in culture in a good way,” says Porch, who, with his wide ice-blue eyes, perfectly smooth head, and perma-smile, looks a bit like how AI would render a human. “What I see every day is that people are externally anti-AI but completely in the closet on how they’re using it. It’s almost like they’re at an AI protest in the morning and then a meeting with me in the afternoon. You know what it reminds me of? The early days of GLP-1’s, when it was like, This is kind of shameful; you’re cheating. But then everyone’s like, Wait, this thing’s incredible.”
